title: July Retail Sales Fall 0.6% — Steepest Drop in Over a Year — as Michigan Sentiment Craters to 51.0; Stocks Slip From Record High
detail: The Census Bureau reported July retail and food-services sales fell 0.6% MoM to $763.6 billion, missing the +0.1% forecast and marking the sharpest monthly decline in more than a year (sales remained up 5.0% YoY). The drop was led by motor vehicle and parts dealers (-1.8%), nonstore/online retailers (-2.2%), and gasoline stations (-0.9%), partly offset by gains in clothing (+1.9%) and health/personal care (+0.7%). Separately, the University of Michigan's preliminary August Consumer Sentiment Index tumbled to 51.0 — a 7.6% MoM decline and 12.4% YoY drop, badly missing the 54.5 consensus and down sharply from July's final 55.2 — with year-ahead inflation expectations rising to 4.3% and short-term expectations falling 11%. The weak-demand, weak-sentiment combination pulled US equities off Thursday's record close: the S&P 500 slipped just below flat, the Dow fell about 0.2%, and the Nasdaq-100 dropped about 0.2%, even after Wednesday's flat PPI and Thursday's cooler CPI had briefly driven stocks to fresh highs.

title: Two UAE Tankers Attacked in Strait of Hormuz — Oil Rebounds to End the Week, Renewing Energy-Shock Risk to Fed Policy
detail: Two ADNOC-operated tankers were struck by drones late Thursday into Friday while transiting the Strait of Hormuz; the UAE's Foreign Ministry blamed Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps, calling the attacks 'acts of piracy' and a 'flagrant violation' of freedom-of-navigation principles. The UK Maritime Trade Operations Center reported both vessels suffered only minor damage with no casualties. It is the second such attack in less than a week — ADNOC reported a similar strike on Aug 8 — bringing the total to 15 ADNOC vessels attacked while transiting the Strait since the US-Israel war with Iran began in February. Oil prices, which had eased earlier in the week alongside the cooler PPI and CPI prints, rebounded to end the week on renewed Gulf supply-risk concerns, re-injecting energy-driven inflation risk into the Fed's rate-path calculus just as soft retail sales and a crumbling consumer-sentiment reading were pulling the recession-risk narrative in the opposite direction.
